general_conventions: M1 = method mark; a later A1 that depends on it cannot be scored without it; in 'show that' items the final A mark is often A0 (the given value earns nothing on its own).
C1 = compensatory method mark, awarded automatically if the final answer is correct; A1 = accuracy mark for the final value; B1 = independent mark for a stated fact or step.

ECF (error carried forward): later numerical parts can earn full credit if consistent with an earlier wrong answer; ECF is allowed after arithmetic (AE), transcription (TE) and power-of-ten (POT) errors but not after wrong physics / wrong equation (XP).
POT: power-of-ten slip (usually an SI-prefix conversion) loses the mark where it occurs, then ECF applies.

SF: giving more significant figures than justified is not penalised; too few is dealt with in individual guidance (often 1 SF is allowed where stated); the SF penalty is applied only once in the paper unless a question explicitly demands a given number of SF.
XP: use of an incorrect equation counts as wrong physics even if it happens to give the right number.
CON: a contradiction within the same response cancels the mark; BOD = benefit of doubt; ^ marks an omission (not wrong but incomplete).

Notation: '/' separates alternatives; Reject/Not = not creditworthy; Ignore = irrelevant extra; Allow = acceptable; words in brackets are not essential; underlined words must be present; AW = alternative wording; ORA = or reverse argument.
General rule for Section B: substitution into an equation may be made with any quantity as subject unless the guidance says otherwise.
Significant figures: if data are given to 2 SF allow answers to 2 or more SF; fewer than 2 SF penalised once only in the whole paper unless guidance says otherwise.
B marks are independent; M marks must be seen and A marks depend on them; C marks can be credited implicitly from correct later working.
MCQ: two responses for a single-answer question score zero; contradictory responses score zero.
Level-of-response guidance (generic): level by science content (best fit), mark within level by the communication statement. No LoR question on this paper (template sentence left as 'X and Y').

Anomalies: MS labels Q24 parts as 24(a)(i) and 24(b)(ii) although the QP has plain 24(a) and 24(b); 26(c) is phrased as 'percentage uncertainty' but is actually a percentage difference from the accepted value.

questions.context: Show power to bulb from three series cells (ε, r each) is 3I(ε − Ir).

questions.context: Why a large internal resistance is undesirable for a torch battery.
questions.answer: More energy wasted as heat inside battery / more lost volts, so less power to bulb.
marking_points: B1: more energy dissipated in r (or larger lost volts / more power I^2r)
B1: so less energy/p.d./power delivered to the bulb
allow_reject_ignore: Ignore references to less current, dimmer bulb or replacing batteries more often.
pitfalls: Only saying 'bulb dimmer' with no energy/p.d. reasoning.

questions.context: Explain why bending knees reduces risk to spine.
questions.answer: Perpendicular distance from load line of action to hips is reduced, so moment smaller, so force on spine smaller.
marking_points: B1: perpendicular distance between weight line and hips reduced
A1: so force on spine reduced
allow_reject_ignore: Allow pivot/fulcrum for hips; allow turning effect.
Ignore centre of mass changes or knees as pivot.
pitfalls: Saying weight is reduced.

questions.context: Describe obtaining enough data (with circuit diagram) to plot thermistor resistance vs temperature as water cools.
questions.answer: Supply with ammeter in series and voltmeter across thermistor; record T, V, I at regular intervals, ≥5 readings; R = V/I.
marking_points: B1: correct circuit — supply, ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel with thermistor
B1: record temperature with thermometer and corresponding V and I as water cools
B1: at least 5 readings / regular intervals
B1: R calculated using R = V/I
allow_reject_ignore: All symbols must be correct; ignore extra components.
pitfalls: Voltmeter in series; wrong thermistor symbol; not stating R = V/I.

questions.context: Use thermistor R–θ graph and LED I–V graph to explain LED switching on above 30 °C.
questions.answer: At 30 °C thermistor ≈30 Ω so LED p.d. = 55/85 × 5 = 3.2 V, above LED turn-on ~3.0 V.
marking_points: C1: LED switches on at about 3.0 V (from I–V graph)
allow_reject_ignore: Alternative: thermistor p.d. 2 V gives 37 Ω, i.e. switches on at ~26 °C.
pitfalls: Not quantifying; mixing which resistor the LED is across.

questions.context: Explain why a falling feather reaches terminal velocity.
questions.answer: Drag grows with speed until it equals weight; resultant force zero, so no acceleration, constant velocity.
allow_reject_ignore: Ignore 'forces balanced' for the second mark.
pitfalls: Saying the weight decreases.

questions.context: Calculate g from three timings of a 2.0 m drop.

questions.topic: 1.1 Practical skills assessed in a written examination
questions.context: Suggest one improvement to the timing investigation.
questions.answer: Use electronic timing (light gates/trap door/video) to remove reaction time, or increase height to reduce % uncertainty in t.
marking_points: M1: electronic timing method (trap door + timer, light gates, video)
OR M1: increase height; A1: longer time reduces % uncertainty
allow_reject_ignore: Improvement must relate to time measurement; ignore 'human error' and 'repeat for range of heights'.
pitfalls: Suggesting only 'repeat and average'.

questions.context: Sketch height vs time from release to first rebound maximum.
questions.answer: Curve down from 2.0 m with increasing steepness to 0, then curve up with decreasing gradient to below 2.0 m at tmax.
marking_points: B1: from 2 m on y-axis, increasingly negative gradient to h = 0
B1: from h = 0, decreasing positive gradient to max below 2 m at tmax
pitfalls: Rebounding to full 2.0 m; straight-line segments.

questions.context: State the meaning of KEmax in Einstein's equation.

questions.context: Explain why the negatively charged electroscope leaf falls under EM radiation.
questions.answer: Electrons absorb photons (one-to-one), are emitted from the plate, so charge falls and leaf drops.
marking_points: B1: electrons emitted from the metal plate/surface
B1: electroscope loses negative charge so leaf falls
allow_reject_ignore: Not emitted from gold leaf; not reference to becoming positive.

questions.context: Explain why below-threshold radiation leaves leaf unchanged.
questions.answer: Photon energy less than work function, so no electron gets enough energy to escape.
marking_points: B1: electron does not gain enough energy to be emitted
pitfalls: Suggesting longer exposure would work.
